subject: math
title: Addition and Subtraction Facts Within 20
seo_title: Grade 2 Addition and Subtraction Facts Worksheets: Make 10, Doubles and Facts Within 20
standard_text: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies. By end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.
meta_desc: Free Grade 2 math facts worksheets: make 10 with ten frames, doubles and near doubles, add by making 10, subtract by thinking addition, and simple word problems. 100 practice questions with step-by-step answers.
key_big: Make 10, use doubles, and think addition to subtract.
key_sub: 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13. 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 + 1 = 13. 13 − 8 = 5 because 8 + 5 = 13. Learn the strategy first, then practice until the facts come from memory.
body_html:
Facts you know by heart

A fact is a sum of two one-digit numbers, like 8 + 5 = 13, and the subtraction that goes with it. By the end of Grade 2, you should know them fast, without counting on your fingers. Three strategies get you there: make 10, doubles and think addition.

Make 10

First learn the pairs that make 10: 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, 4 + 6 and 5 + 5. Then fill up a 10 to add a bigger fact.

Example

9 + 6 = ?

9 needs 1 to make 10. Take 1 from the 6, and 5 is left. 10 + 5 = 15.

Answer: 15

Doubles and near doubles

A double adds a number to itself: 6 + 6 = 12. A near double is 1 more: 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 and 1 more, so 6 + 7 = 13.

DoubleNear double
5 + 5 = 105 + 6 = 11
6 + 6 = 126 + 7 = 13
7 + 7 = 147 + 8 = 15
8 + 8 = 168 + 9 = 17
9 + 9 = 189 + 10 = 19

Subtract: think addition

To find 13 − 8, ask: 8 + what = 13? Count up from 8. Jump to 10, then to 13.

Fact family

6, 9 and 15

6 + 9 = 15, 9 + 6 = 15, 15 − 9 = 6, 15 − 6 = 9. If you know one fact, you know all four.

Answer: 4 facts from 1 family

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting the start number: 12 − 3 → “12, 11, 10”, so 10Start at 12 and say the next number: 11, 10, 9. 12 − 3 = 9
Forgetting to take away when making 10: 9 + 4 → 14If 1 goes to the 9, only 3 is left: 10 + 3 = 13
Adding when the story says take awayWords like “fly away”, “are left” and “give” mean subtract
Getting a double wrong by 2: 7 + 7 = 12Remember a picture: two weeks have 14 days, so 7 + 7 = 14
Using the wrong double: 6 + 7 → 7 + 7 + 1Double the smaller number and add 1: 6 + 6 + 1 = 13

faq.q: What math facts should a 2nd grader know by heart?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 2, children should know all sums of two one-digit numbers from memory, like 8 + 7 = 15 (Common Core 2.OA.B.2). They should also add and subtract within 20 quickly, using strategies such as making 10.

faq.q: What is the make a 10 strategy?
faq.a: Break one number apart to fill a 10 first. For 8 + 5, take 2 from the 5 so 8 + 2 = 10, then add the 3 that is left: 10 + 3 = 13.

faq.q: What are doubles and near doubles in math?
faq.a: Doubles are facts that add a number to itself, like 6 + 6 = 12. Near doubles are one more, like 6 + 7: use the double and add 1, so 6 + 7 = 13.

faq.q: How can my child learn math facts without counting on fingers?
faq.a: Teach one strategy at a time (make 10, doubles, think addition) and practice a few facts for about 5 minutes every day. Saying the whole fact out loud, like “9 + 6 = 15”, helps it move into memory.

items.q: 4 + 4 = ?
items.e: 4 + 4 is a double. 4 + 4 = 8. A spider has 8 legs: 4 on each side.

items.q: 5 + 5 = ?
items.e: 5 + 5 is a double. 5 + 5 = 10. Two hands have 10 fingers: 5 and 5.

items.q: 6 + 6 = ?
items.e: 6 + 6 is a double. 6 + 6 = 12. An egg carton has 2 rows of 6 eggs: 12 eggs.
7 + 7 is a double. 7 + 7 = 14. Two weeks have 14 days: 7 and 7.

9 + 9 is a double. 9 + 9 = 18. 10 + 10 = 20. Take away 2, and you get 18.

items.q: Use a double. 5 + 6 = ?
items.e: 5 + 5 = 10. 6 is 1 more than 5, so add 1 more: 10 + 1 = 11.
8 + 8 = 16. 9 is 1 more than 8, so add 1 more: 16 + 1 = 17.

items.q: Use a double. 4 + 5 = ?
items.e: 4 + 4 = 8. 5 is 1 more than 4, so add 1 more: 8 + 1 = 9.
7 + 7 = 14. 8 is 1 more than 7, so add 1 more: 14 + 1 = 15.

items.q: Which way uses a double to find 8 + 9?
items.e: 9 is 1 more than 8. So 8 + 9 is 8 + 8 and 1 more: 16 + 1 = 17.

items.q: Which way uses a double to find 7 + 6?
items.e: 7 is 1 more than 6. So 7 + 6 is 6 + 6 and 1 more: 12 + 1 = 13.

items.q: Which way uses a double to find 3 + 4?
items.e: 4 is 1 more than 3. So 3 + 4 is 3 + 3 and 1 more: 6 + 1 = 7.

items.q: Which way uses a double to find 6 + 5?
items.e: 6 is 1 more than 5. So 6 + 5 is 5 + 5 and 1 more: 10 + 1 = 11.

items.q: Owen knows 8 + 8 = 16. How can he find 8 + 7?
items.e: 7 is 1 less than 8. So 8 + 7 is 1 less than 8 + 8: 16 − 1 = 15.

5 + 5 = 10. 7 is 2 more than 5, so add 2: 10 + 2 = 12. Or use the middle number: 6 + 6 = 12.
7 + 7 = 14. 9 is 2 more than 7, so add 2: 14 + 2 = 16. Or use the middle number: 8 + 8 = 16.
4 + 4 = 8. 6 is 2 more than 4, so add 2: 8 + 2 = 10. Or use the middle number: 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: Which fact is in the same family as 6 + 9 = 15?
items.e: The family of 6, 9 and 15: 6 + 9 = 15, 9 + 6 = 15, 15 − 6 = 9, 15 − 9 = 6. Only 15 − 9 = 6 uses all three numbers.

items.q: Which fact is in the same family as 7 + 5 = 12?
items.e: The family of 7, 5 and 12: 7 + 5 = 12, 5 + 7 = 12, 12 − 7 = 5, 12 − 5 = 7. Only 12 − 7 = 5 uses all three numbers.

items.q: Which fact is in the same family as 8 + 9 = 17?
items.e: The family of 8, 9 and 17: 8 + 9 = 17, 9 + 8 = 17, 17 − 8 = 9, 17 − 9 = 8. Only 9 + 8 = 17 uses all three numbers.

items.q: Ava has 8 red beads and 5 blue beads. How many beads does she have?
items.e: Put the two groups together, so add. Take 2 from the 5 to make 10: 8 + 2 = 10. Then add the 3 left: 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: There are 15 birds on a fence. 7 birds fly away. How many birds are left?
items.e: Some are gone, so subtract: 15 − 7 = 8. Think: 7 + 8 = 15.

items.q: Nora has 9 toy cars. She gets 3 more. How many toy cars does she have now?
items.e: Put the two groups together, so add. Take 1 from the 3 to make 10: 9 + 1 = 10. Then add the 2 left: 10 + 2 = 12.

items.q: There are 12 apples in a bag. Ben uses 4 for a pie. How many apples are left?
items.e: Some are gone, so subtract: 12 − 4 = 8. Think: 4 + 8 = 12.

items.q: A tank has 6 fish. The class puts in 7 more fish. How many fish are in the tank now?
items.e: Put the two groups together, so add. Start with 7. Take 3 from the 6 to make 10: 7 + 3 = 10. Then add the 3 left: 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: Zoe has 16 stickers. She gives 9 to a friend. How many stickers does she have left?
items.e: Some are gone, so subtract: 16 − 9 = 7. Think: 9 + 7 = 16.

items.q: Omar read 7 pages on Monday. He read 7 pages on Tuesday. How many pages did he read in all?
items.e: Put the pages together, so add: 7 + 7 = 14. It is a double.

items.q: There are 11 kids at the park. 5 kids go home. How many kids are still at the park?
items.e: Some are gone, so subtract: 11 − 5 = 6. Think: 5 + 6 = 11.

items.q: Ruby has 9 crayons. She wants 15 crayons. How many more crayons does she need?
items.e: Count up from 9 to 15: 9 + 6 = 15. So 15 − 9 = 6.

items.q: Luis has 13 shells. Jack has 6 shells. How many more shells does Luis have than Jack?
items.e: Find the difference: 13 − 6 = 7. Think: 6 + 7 = 13.

items.q: There are 14 cookies on a plate. The kids eat some. Now 8 cookies are left. How many cookies did they eat?
items.e: Some are gone, so subtract: 14 − 8 = 6. Think: 8 + 6 = 14.

items.q: Some ducks are in a pond. 4 more ducks come. Now there are 11 ducks. How many ducks were there at first?
items.e: Take away the 4 ducks that came: 11 − 4 = 7. Check: 7 + 4 = 11.

items.q: There are 17 children on a bus. 8 children get off. How many children are on the bus now?
items.e: Some are gone, so subtract: 17 − 8 = 9. Think: 8 + 9 = 17.

items.q: Grace picks 6 flowers. Maya picks 8 flowers. How many flowers do they pick in all?
items.e: Put the two groups together, so add. Start with 8. Take 2 from the 6 to make 10: 8 + 2 = 10. Then add the 4 left: 10 + 4 = 14.
